messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that distinguishes genuine utterance ambiguity from model uncertainty under unseen compositional structures. The targets are ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, evaluated using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, and unambiguous-input execution accuracy that matches a single-output parser trained on identical data.

Those are two distinct requirements. The first concerns whether the parser recognizes when an utterance genuinely admits multiple valid interpretations, rather than treating its own uncertainty as evidence of ambiguity. The second requires that this capability not come at the expense of execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs, relative to the single-output parser trained on identical data.
Can you sharpen the distinction between genuine ambiguity and uncertainty? They can look similar if a parser hesitates between interpretations.

They can look similar from the parser’s perspective, but the distinction is about the utterance, not merely the parser’s confidence. Genuine ambiguity means more than one interpretation is valid for that utterance. Model uncertainty means the parser is unsure which interpretation is valid; that uncertainty alone does not establish that multiple interpretations are valid.
So producing several candidates would not, by itself, count as detecting ambiguity?

Right. Several candidates could reflect uncertainty about a single valid interpretation. Ambiguity detection has to distinguish that situation from an utterance with multiple valid interpretations. The independently annotated sets of valid interpretations provide the reference for that distinction in the stated evaluation.
What role does the independent annotation play here?

It keeps the determination of valid interpretations separate from the parser’s own guesses. The ambiguity-detection target is assessed using those independently annotated sets, rather than assuming that whatever alternatives the parser produces are all valid. The goal does not specify an annotation procedure beyond that independence and the use of sets of valid interpretations.
And the ≥0.85 figure applies specifically to ambiguity-detection F1 on unseen compositions?

Yes. The numerical requirement is ambiguity-detection F1 of at least 0.85 on unseen compositions, using the independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. It is not stated as a threshold for every other measure, and it does not give separate minimum values for precision and recall.
Why emphasize unseen compositional structures rather than just asking whether the parser recognizes ambiguity in general?

The goal specifically calls for the distinction to hold under unseen compositional structures. That focuses the requirement on cases where the composition is unseen, not merely on the parser’s ability to recognize ambiguity in familiar cases. It does not, by itself, specify a particular kind of composition or say how those unseen cases are constructed.
Could a parser be very uncertain about an unseen composition while the utterance is still unambiguous?

Yes. Encountering an unseen structure may leave the parser unsure, but that does not change how many interpretations of the utterance are actually valid. The intended distinction is precisely between uncertainty in the model and ambiguity in the utterance.
Does the goal require a particular way to represent multiple interpretations?

No particular representation or parser architecture is stated. The requirement is about the distinction the parser must make and the two performance comparisons it must satisfy. The sets of valid interpretations are specified as the independently annotated evaluation reference, not as a mandated internal representation.
Let me check the second condition. It is about execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs, not just whether the parser labels those inputs unambiguous, correct?

Correct. The second condition explicitly concerns unambiguous-input execution accuracy. Recognizing that an input is unambiguous would not, on its own, satisfy a requirement to match the execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data.
Does ‘trained on identical data’ qualify the baseline comparison?

Yes. The comparison is to a single-output parser trained on identical data. That condition keeps the stated accuracy comparison tied to the same training data; the goal does not supply a numerical accuracy value for the baseline or prescribe its architecture beyond calling it a single-output parser.
Could we accept a drop in unambiguous-input execution accuracy if the ambiguity F1 exceeds 0.85?

Not under the stated goal. Achieving ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions is one requirement, and matching the baseline’s unambiguous-input execution accuracy is another. Exceeding the F1 threshold does not remove the separate accuracy condition.
Likewise, matching the baseline on unambiguous inputs would not compensate for poor ambiguity detection?

Exactly. Matching that execution accuracy addresses only the unambiguous-input comparison. The parser must also reach ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions when evaluated using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations.
I want to avoid calling every difficult utterance ambiguous. Is that the main conceptual boundary?

Yes. Difficulty for the parser is not the same thing as multiple valid meanings in the utterance. The goal is to preserve that boundary even under unseen compositional structures, while also preserving the specified execution-accuracy comparison on unambiguous inputs.
Then the intended outcome is a parser that can make that distinction without losing the performance a single-output parser has on clear inputs?

That captures it, with the targets stated precisely: ambiguity-detection F1 must be at least 0.85 on unseen compositions, assessed using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, and unambiguous-input execution accuracy must match that of a single-output parser trained on identical data.

For the parser we discussed, I’d propose training a shared encoder with an execution head and an interpretation-set head on annotated parse sets. Ambiguity would be detected from predicted set cardinality, not from entropy.

That proposal gives the two concerns distinct outputs while sharing an encoder. The execution head addresses execution; the interpretation-set head addresses which interpretations are valid. Ambiguity detection would then depend on how many valid interpretations the latter predicts, rather than on how uncertain the model is about its predictions.
Can you spell out what ‘predicted cardinality’ means in this setting?

It is the predicted number of valid interpretations in the interpretation set. A prediction of one valid interpretation points to an unambiguous utterance; a prediction of more than one points to genuine ambiguity. The important qualification is ‘valid’: merely generating several possible parses is not the same as predicting that several belong in the valid set.
Why not use entropy as the ambiguity signal? It seems like a convenient measure of how divided the model is.

Entropy describes uncertainty in a prediction distribution. A model could be divided between candidates because it cannot tell which single one is correct, even when the utterance has only one valid interpretation. Conversely, the question for ambiguity detection is whether multiple interpretations are valid, not whether the model feels uncertain. The proposal therefore bases the decision on predicted set cardinality instead.
So high entropy would not automatically mean an utterance is ambiguous?
Correct. High entropy can reflect model uncertainty. Under this proposal, ambiguity is indicated by a predicted interpretation set containing more than one valid member, not by high entropy alone.
And low entropy wouldn’t be a substitute for predicting the set either?

Right. Confidence and cardinality answer different questions. Even a confident prediction does not, by itself, establish whether the utterance admits one valid interpretation or several. The interpretation-set head is meant to make that distinction explicitly.
What does sharing the encoder contribute to the proposal?

It means the execution and interpretation-set heads draw on a common encoded representation of the input. The proposal couples the two tasks at that level while leaving each head responsible for its own output. It does not specify an encoder architecture or claim that sharing alone will achieve either performance target.
Is the interpretation-set head just another way of making the execution head output several answers?

Not necessarily. The proposal names separate heads because an execution output and a set of valid interpretations serve different purposes. In particular, the interpretation-set head supplies the set whose predicted cardinality is used for ambiguity detection. The proposal does not specify how an execution should be selected or represented when an utterance has multiple valid interpretations.
What does training on annotated parse sets add, as opposed to training only on a single parse per utterance?

Annotated parse sets provide supervision about which interpretations belong to the valid set, including when there is more than one. That is directly relevant to learning an interpretation-set prediction. A single parse alone would not, merely by being present, say whether other interpretations are also valid. The proposal does not prescribe the annotation process or the precise training objective.
If the interpretation-set head predicts several parses and only one is actually valid, what happens to the ambiguity judgment?

On the proposed cardinality rule, predicting several as valid would produce an ambiguity judgment, but it would be an error relative to the actual valid-interpretation set. The distinction still depends on correctly predicting validity, not simply on counting whatever candidates the model can produce.
And if it misses one of two valid interpretations?

If it predicts only one valid interpretation where there are two, its predicted cardinality would fail to indicate the genuine ambiguity. Those two cases show why the quality of the predicted set matters to ambiguity detection; cardinality is the decision signal, not a guarantee that the decision is correct.
Does this proposal change the requirement to preserve execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs?

No. The execution head is part of the proposed approach, but the requirement remains that unambiguous-input execution accuracy match that of a single-output parser trained on identical data. Having an execution head does not establish that the requirement has been met.
Nor does choosing cardinality over entropy establish the ambiguity-detection score, I assume?

Exactly. It specifies how the proposed parser would decide whether to flag ambiguity. Whether it reaches ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, remains a performance question, not a result implied by the proposal.
Could I describe the proposal as separating ‘what should execute’ from ‘how many readings are valid,’ without claiming they are unrelated?

Yes, provided the description retains the shared encoder and the interpretation-set output. The heads address different questions, but they are part of one proposed parser and use a shared representation. ‘How many readings are valid’ is determined from the predicted interpretation set, not from an uncertainty statistic.
Does the proposal require the interpretation-set head to output a confidence threshold for each parse?

It does not specify a thresholding rule or another particular mechanism for forming the predicted set. What it does specify is an interpretation-set head trained on annotated parse sets and an ambiguity decision based on predicted cardinality rather than entropy. The details of how that head produces its set are left open.
Then the central idea is not that uncertainty disappears. It’s that uncertainty is not treated as proof of multiple valid interpretations.

That’s the distinction. The model can still be uncertain, but under this proposal its ambiguity judgment comes from the number of interpretations it predicts as valid. That keeps the proposed signal aligned with utterance ambiguity rather than equating ambiguity with hesitation.
Can supervised interpretation-set cardinality distinguish genuine alternative parses from high-entropy errors on unseen compositions?

It could provide that distinction, but the question is whether it does so reliably on unseen compositions. Predicted cardinality asks how many interpretations the parser judges valid. Entropy asks how uncertain the parser is. Those are different quantities, so cardinality gives the parser a way to represent genuine alternatives without treating uncertainty itself as ambiguity. Supervision on annotated parse sets does not, by itself, establish that the distinction will generalize.
What would the distinction look like when an error has high entropy?

The parser might be unsure which of several parses is right even though only one is valid. That is high uncertainty about a single valid answer. If its interpretation-set prediction contains just that one valid parse, its cardinality-based ambiguity judgment remains unambiguous despite the uncertainty. If it mistakenly includes other parses as valid, however, cardinality will produce a false ambiguity judgment.
So cardinality does not magically filter out errors. It depends on what gets counted.

Exactly. The relevant count is the number of interpretations predicted to be valid, not the number the parser considered. Supervision on interpretation sets gives the model information about that distinction, but an incorrect set prediction can still turn uncertainty into an incorrect ambiguity judgment.
What about the other direction: a genuinely ambiguous utterance for which the parser is confident in only one parse?

If the parser predicts only one valid interpretation, its predicted cardinality would indicate no ambiguity, even though another interpretation is valid. Its confidence in the one parse would not resolve that omission. Distinguishing genuine alternatives requires the predicted set to include them, not merely to avoid being uncertain.
Then is entropy irrelevant, or just the wrong basis for the ambiguity decision?

Here it is the wrong basis for deciding whether multiple interpretations are valid. Entropy can describe the model’s uncertainty, but high uncertainty is not proof of genuine alternatives, and low uncertainty is not proof that alternatives do not exist. The question is whether supervised set cardinality tracks the valid interpretations more faithfully on unseen compositions.
Why does ‘unseen compositions’ make that an open question?

The proposed supervision concerns valid parse sets, while the question asks whether the learned distinction carries over when the compositional structure is unseen. A parser could have learned to predict cardinality on its training examples yet make set-membership mistakes on unfamiliar combinations. Nothing in the proposal alone settles how accurately it will predict the valid set in those cases.
Is the key uncertainty here whether it predicts the right number, or whether it predicts the right parses?

For the ambiguity judgment, the immediate signal is the predicted number. But that number is meaningful only insofar as the predicted set reflects genuinely valid interpretations. A set containing two parses when only one is valid gives the wrong ambiguity judgment; a set containing one when two are valid misses ambiguity. Predicting the right number and predicting the right members are closely related, though they are not identical claims.
Could it predict the right cardinality for the wrong reasons?

Yes. A predicted set could have the same size as the valid set while containing a wrong parse or omitting a valid one. That would leave the count unchanged but would not mean the interpretation set itself was correct. The narrow ambiguity decision might agree with the reference in that instance, while the broader claim that the parser recovered the genuine alternatives would not follow.
So when I ask whether cardinality can distinguish alternatives from high-entropy errors, I should not equate a correct binary judgment with a correct interpretation set?

Right. A correct ambiguity judgment says that the predicted cardinality falls on the right side of the one-versus-multiple distinction. Recovering the actual valid alternatives is a stronger claim. Independently annotated sets of valid interpretations make it possible to keep those claims conceptually separate.
How does supervision help without guaranteeing either claim?

Annotated parse sets tell the parser which interpretations are valid together, rather than supplying only one parse and leaving the status of alternatives unspecified. That is relevant supervision for predicting set membership and cardinality. Whether the parser uses it successfully on unseen compositions remains the open part of your question.
Would a high-entropy prediction ever be evidence of ambiguity on its own?

Not on its own. It is evidence that the model is uncertain among possibilities, but it does not establish that more than one possibility is a valid reading of the utterance. The independently annotated valid-interpretation set, rather than the model’s hesitation, determines whether the utterance is genuinely ambiguous.
And a low-entropy prediction would not rule ambiguity out?

Correct. The parser could be confident in one interpretation and still overlook another valid one. Entropy describes how its belief is distributed; ambiguity concerns the utterance’s valid interpretations.
Does the shared encoder with separate execution and interpretation-set heads affect the answer to this question?

It identifies where the cardinality prediction comes from in the proposal: the interpretation-set head uses the shared representation to predict a set, while the execution head addresses execution. That arrangement does not itself show whether the set head will separate genuine alternatives from high-entropy errors under unseen compositions. The question turns on the resulting set predictions.
If the cardinality signal works on familiar structures, can I infer it will work on unseen compositions?

No. Success on familiar structures would not, by itself, answer the question about unseen compositions. The issue is specifically whether the learned distinction between valid alternatives and uncertainty persists under those unseen structures.
What is the most careful short answer to the question, then?

Supervised interpretation-set cardinality is a plausible way to distinguish genuine alternative parses from high-entropy errors because it targets the number of valid interpretations rather than uncertainty. Whether it actually makes that distinction on unseen compositions is unresolved without knowing how accurately it predicts the valid sets there.

I’d frame a hypothesis for unseen COGS-AMB compositions: cardinality supervision yields ambiguity F1 ≥0.85, exceeds entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10 in ambiguity F1, and does not reduce unambiguous execution accuracy.

That is a hypothesis, not an observed result. It makes three claims together: ambiguity F1 reaches at least 0.85 on unseen COGS-AMB compositions; its ambiguity F1 is at least 0.10 higher than entropy-thresholding’s; and the gain does not come with reduced execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs.
Is the ≥0.10 comparison another way of stating the ≥0.85 target?

No. The ≥0.85 condition is an absolute ambiguity-F1 target. The ≥0.10 condition is a difference between the ambiguity F1 from cardinality supervision and the ambiguity F1 from entropy-thresholding. One condition does not automatically imply the other.
So I should keep both numbers when I state the hypothesis?

Yes. Saying only that cardinality supervision reaches ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 would omit the comparison with entropy-thresholding. Saying only that it exceeds entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10 would omit the absolute ≥0.85 target.
What is entropy-thresholding doing in this comparison?

It is the comparison approach for ambiguity detection: using an entropy threshold as the signal, rather than basing the ambiguity judgment on predicted interpretation-set cardinality. The hypothesis says cardinality supervision will outperform that approach in ambiguity F1 on unseen COGS-AMB compositions. It does not specify a particular threshold value.
Is the hypothesized advantage just that cardinality and entropy measure different things?

That distinction motivates the hypothesis, but it does not prove the advantage. Cardinality aims to capture how many parses are valid, whereas entropy reflects uncertainty among predictions. The claim that this distinction produces ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 and an advantage of ≥0.10 over entropy-thresholding on unseen COGS-AMB compositions remains to be established.
If the parser is highly uncertain about an utterance with only one valid parse, what does the hypothesis suggest?

It suggests that supervision on valid interpretation sets could help the parser avoid treating that uncertainty as genuine ambiguity. But it does not say the parser will get every such utterance right. The stated prediction is about ambiguity F1 and its comparison with entropy-thresholding across unseen COGS-AMB compositions, not a guarantee for each input.
And the converse would be recognizing multiple valid parses even if uncertainty alone is a poor cue?

Yes, that is the other side of the proposed distinction. If multiple parses are genuinely valid, an interpretation-set prediction with cardinality greater than one can express that directly. The hypothesis is that cardinality supervision will make this signal effective enough to meet the stated F1 target and outperform entropy-thresholding by the stated margin.
Could the cardinality approach meet ≥0.85 but still fail the hypothesis?
Yes. It could meet the absolute F1 target without exceeding entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10, or it could reduce unambiguous execution accuracy. All three conditions are part of the hypothesis.
Could it beat entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10 yet still fall short?

Yes. A difference of at least 0.10 would satisfy the comparative claim, but the cardinality-supervised approach would still need ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 on unseen COGS-AMB compositions and no reduction in unambiguous execution accuracy.
The execution clause seems separate from the ambiguity comparison. Why include it?

It rules out treating an ambiguity-detection gain as sufficient if execution on unambiguous inputs gets worse. The broader parser goal calls for preserving unambiguous-input execution accuracy relative to a single-output parser trained on identical data. The hypothesis likewise says the proposed ambiguity gain should occur without reducing unambiguous execution accuracy.
Does this hypothesis claim an improvement in unambiguous execution accuracy?

No. ‘Without reducing’ states that accuracy should not fall; it does not predict that accuracy will rise. The proposed improvement is in ambiguity detection relative to entropy-thresholding, alongside preservation of unambiguous execution accuracy.
Should I describe the ≥0.10 difference as a relative ten-percent improvement?

That would change the claim. The stated comparison is an ambiguity-F1 difference of at least 0.10, not a relative percentage increase. Keeping it as ‘exceeds entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10 in ambiguity F1’ avoids that ambiguity.
Does ‘unseen’ qualify both the absolute target and the comparison?

Yes. The hypothesis is specifically about unseen COGS-AMB compositions. Both the predicted ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 and the predicted ≥0.10 advantage over entropy-thresholding concern that setting. It does not make a separate claim about familiar compositions.
Do we know from the hypothesis what particular compositions are in COGS-AMB?
No. COGS-AMB names the setting in the hypothesis, but the statement does not enumerate its compositions or specify how they were constructed. Those details should not be inferred from the name alone.
Is there any result here that tells us the prediction is already correct?

No result is stated. This node expresses a testable expectation: cardinality supervision will achieve ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 on unseen COGS-AMB compositions, beat entropy-thresholding by ≥0.10 in ambiguity F1, and do so without reducing unambiguous execution accuracy.

Then the strongest careful phrasing is that set-cardinality supervision is predicted to separate genuine alternatives from uncertainty better than entropy-thresholding in that setting, while preserving execution on unambiguous inputs?

Yes, so long as the quantitative claims remain explicit and predictive: on unseen COGS-AMB compositions, the hypothesized ambiguity F1 is ≥0.85 and ≥0.10 above entropy-thresholding’s ambiguity F1, without reducing unambiguous execution accuracy. That wording does not present the hypothesis as a measured outcome.

To address whether supervised interpretation-set cardinality can distinguish genuine alternatives from high-entropy errors, I’d independently annotate COGS-AMB interpretation sets, train cardinality and single-output parsers on matched data, then compare cardinality-versus-entropy ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy on novel compositions.

That lays out a comparison without treating the question as already answered. The independent COGS-AMB annotations establish which interpretations are valid; the matched-data parsers support the execution-accuracy comparison; and the evaluation on novel compositions asks whether cardinality-based ambiguity detection differs from entropy-based detection where the compositions are unseen.
What exactly needs to be in the independent annotations?

For this plan, they need to identify sets of valid interpretations for the COGS-AMB utterances. That matters because the reference must distinguish an utterance with genuinely multiple valid parses from one for which a parser merely has several uncertain guesses. The plan does not specify the annotation procedure or a particular format for the sets.
Could the parser’s own candidate list serve as the reference set?

Not as a substitute for independent annotation. A candidate list shows what the parser produced, which may include invalid alternatives or omit valid ones. Independently annotated sets supply a separate basis for judging whether the utterance is ambiguous.
When I say ‘train matched-data cardinality and single-output parsers,’ what comparison am I preserving?

You are preserving the comparison of unambiguous-input execution accuracy against a single-output parser trained on identical data. ‘Matched-data’ is important because the execution comparison should not be attributed to the parsers having different training data. The plan does not state further details about their architectures or training procedures.
Is the single-output parser the entropy-thresholding comparator too?

The plan identifies two comparisons, but it does not specify that those comparators must be the same parser. Cardinality versus entropy concerns how ambiguity is detected and compared by F1. Cardinality versus the single-output parser concerns execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. It would go beyond the stated plan to assign the entropy-thresholding approach a particular architecture.
That distinction is useful. How should I describe the two measurements without blending them?

Describe ambiguity-detection F1 for cardinality-based detection versus entropy-based detection on novel compositions. Separately, describe unambiguous-input execution accuracy for the cardinality parser versus the matched-data single-output parser. F1 addresses whether ambiguity is detected; execution accuracy addresses whether clear inputs are executed correctly.
Does the plan say to measure execution accuracy only on novel compositions as well?

The stated comparison places both ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy on novel compositions. Within that setting, execution accuracy concerns the unambiguous inputs. The plan does not describe additional evaluations on familiar compositions.
Why is the annotation independent if the approach is also trained on annotated parse sets?

The two statements concern different roles for annotations. The proposed cardinality approach uses annotated parse sets for supervision, while independent annotation provides a reference for which interpretations are valid when assessing ambiguity. The plan does not specify exactly how annotations are allocated between training and evaluation, so it is best not to infer a particular allocation.
Could I say the evaluation checks whether the parser is simply uncertain whenever it predicts multiple parses?

More precisely, it checks whether the parser’s ambiguity decisions align with independently annotated valid-interpretation sets on novel compositions. If several parses are predicted but the annotated set contains only one valid interpretation, calling that utterance ambiguous would mistake model uncertainty or error for genuine ambiguity. If the annotated set contains multiple valid interpretations, the ambiguity judgment should reflect that.
So entropy F1 is included to test the specific concern about high-entropy errors?

Yes. Comparing cardinality-based and entropy-based ambiguity F1 speaks directly to whether predicting the number of valid interpretations distinguishes ambiguity more effectively than using an uncertainty signal. The plan calls for the comparison; it does not state which method will score higher.
And the execution comparison prevents an ambiguity-focused approach from looking successful while doing worse on clear inputs?

It makes that trade-off visible. The plan includes unambiguous execution accuracy alongside ambiguity F1, using the matched-data single-output parser for the relevant baseline comparison. It does not report whether execution accuracy is maintained.
Should I put the earlier numerical targets into the plan, or would that make it sound like results?

You can retain them as criteria, not outcomes. The goal is ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions and unambiguous-input execution accuracy matching a single-output parser trained on identical data. The hypothesis also predicts an ambiguity-F1 advantage of ≥0.10 over entropy-thresholding on unseen COGS-AMB compositions without reduced unambiguous execution accuracy. This plan describes comparisons that can address those claims; it does not establish that any threshold or comparison has been met.
Does ‘novel compositions’ mean I need to make a claim about every type of unseen structure?

No. It names the setting for the planned comparisons, not a guarantee about every possible unseen structure. The plan does not enumerate composition types or claim results beyond the compositions that would be evaluated.
Would a strong cardinality-versus-entropy F1 comparison alone answer the whole question?

It would address the ambiguity-detection part of the question on novel compositions, relative to entropy-based detection. The independently annotated sets are important for interpreting that comparison as genuine ambiguity detection. The plan also checks unambiguous execution accuracy, because success at distinguishing ambiguity should not be conflated with performance on execution.
Suppose a cardinality prediction has the right count but the wrong parses. Would the plan let us call the predicted interpretations correct?

No. The count could support a correct ambiguity judgment without identifying the correct members of the valid set. Independent interpretation-set annotations preserve that distinction. The stated ambiguity-F1 comparison concerns detection, so it should not be described as proof that every predicted interpretation is correct.
What, then, is the most faithful one-sentence description of the work to do?

Independently annotate valid-interpretation sets for COGS-AMB, train cardinality and single-output parsers on matched data, and compare cardinality-based versus entropy-based ambiguity F1 and unambiguous-input execution accuracy on novel compositions.
And until those comparisons are made, the claim that cardinality separates genuine ambiguity from high-entropy errors remains a question rather than a finding?
Yes. The plan is designed to examine that question against independent valid-interpretation sets while checking execution on unambiguous inputs; it does not supply the comparison results.

The next activity is to run five-seed COGS-AMB novel-composition splits and compare the cardinality, entropy, and matched-data single-output baselines on ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy.

That sets out the evaluation activity without stating an outcome. The five-seed runs provide repeated comparisons on novel compositions. Ambiguity F1 addresses detection of genuine ambiguity, while unambiguous execution accuracy checks performance on inputs with a single valid interpretation.
I want to be precise about ‘five-seed.’ Does that mean five kinds of ambiguity?

No. ‘Five-seed’ describes the repeated runs of the COGS-AMB novel-composition splits. It does not say there are five ambiguity types or five kinds of composition. The activity does not specify the seeds themselves or how the splits are generated.
What should remain constant when I describe the comparison?

Keep the evaluation setting explicit: COGS-AMB novel-composition splits, run with five seeds. Also retain the matched-data condition for the single-output baseline. Beyond those stated conditions, the activity does not prescribe particular training settings or implementation details.
Are cardinality and entropy being compared on ambiguity F1 because they provide different ambiguity signals?

Yes. The cardinality approach bases an ambiguity judgment on the predicted number of valid interpretations; the entropy approach uses a model-uncertainty signal. Comparing their ambiguity F1 on novel compositions addresses whether those signals differ in how well they identify genuine ambiguity.
Where does the single-output baseline fit? I don’t want to blur the two metrics.

It is the matched-data comparison for execution on unambiguous inputs. The activity names cardinality, entropy, and the matched-data single-output baseline in the overall comparison, with ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy as the two measures. It does not specify a particular method for deriving ambiguity decisions from the single-output baseline, so that detail should not be assumed.
Would it be accurate to say this activity tests the predicted advantage over entropy-thresholding?

Yes, as a purpose of the comparison rather than a result. Ambiguity F1 on the novel-composition splits can be compared between cardinality and entropy. The earlier hypothesis predicts cardinality F1 ≥0.85 and an advantage of ≥0.10 over entropy-thresholding on unseen COGS-AMB compositions, but this activity states no measured F1 values.
And unambiguous execution accuracy checks the other part of that hypothesis?

Yes. It checks whether ambiguity detection is accompanied by reduced execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. The matched-data single-output baseline supplies the execution comparison. Nothing in the activity says whether accuracy is preserved or reduced.
Why specify novel-composition splits in the activity rather than simply saying ‘evaluate on COGS-AMB’?

Because the question concerns performance under unseen compositional structures. ‘Novel-composition splits’ identifies the setting in which these ambiguity and execution comparisons are to be made. Saying only ‘on COGS-AMB’ would leave out that condition.
Does running five seeds itself demonstrate that the parser generalizes?

No. Five-seed evaluation describes how the comparisons are run repeatedly; it is not a performance result. Whether the ambiguity and execution measures support a generalization claim depends on their observed values on those novel-composition splits.
Should I expect one ambiguity F1 number or five?

The activity calls for five-seed runs, so ambiguity F1 can be examined for each run. It does not specify how those results should be combined or reported as a single number. We should not assume a particular aggregation rule.
The same caution applies to unambiguous execution accuracy?
Yes. It is a measure to compare across the five-seed novel-composition runs, but the activity does not prescribe an aggregation method or supply any accuracy values.
Can I say an entropy method is wrong whenever its F1 is lower than cardinality’s?

A lower ambiguity F1 would indicate weaker ambiguity detection under the stated comparison, not that every entropy-based decision is wrong. The activity is to compare measured performance; it does not make a blanket claim about individual utterances or report which approach scores higher.
And if cardinality has high ambiguity F1, that still leaves execution accuracy to check?

Correct. Ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy measure different requirements. A favorable result on one would not establish a favorable result on the other, which is why this activity includes both.
Does ‘matched-data’ mean the single-output parser has the same outputs as the cardinality parser?

No. It qualifies the data used for the comparison, not the form of the parsers’ outputs. The single-output baseline remains a single-output parser. The activity does not specify that it shares the cardinality parser’s architecture or interpretation-set output.
How do the independently annotated valid-interpretation sets relate to these runs?

They provide the reference for identifying genuine ambiguity when ambiguity F1 is assessed. The five-seed activity describes the runs and comparisons; it does not add details about how those sets were annotated or allocated among splits.
So I should avoid describing any F1 or accuracy figures as already observed here?
Yes. ‘Run’ and ‘compare’ state the activity to perform. No resulting ambiguity F1, difference from entropy, or unambiguous execution accuracy is given in this node.
What’s a compact but complete way to state the activity?

Run five-seed COGS-AMB novel-composition splits, comparing cardinality-based and entropy-based ambiguity detection alongside a matched-data single-output baseline, and assess ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution accuracy without presuming the results.
The five COGS-AMB seeds produced these results: cardinality achieved ambiguity F1 of 0.87 versus 0.74 for entropy, and unambiguous execution accuracy matched the single-output parser at 91%.

Across those five seeds, the reported ambiguity-F1 difference is 0.13 in favor of cardinality. The execution result is a separate comparison: on unambiguous inputs, the cardinality parser and the single-output parser both achieved 91% accuracy.
When you say 0.13, is that the difference between the two F1 scores?
Yes. Subtracting entropy’s 0.74 from cardinality’s 0.87 gives an absolute F1 difference of 0.13. It is not a claim of a 13% relative increase.
I want to keep ambiguity detection and execution distinct. Which numbers belong to which measure?

The F1 scores—0.87 for cardinality and 0.74 for entropy—concern ambiguity detection. The 91% figure concerns execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs, where the cardinality parser matched the single-output parser.
Does the 91% figure mean entropy also had 91% unambiguous execution accuracy?

That is not stated. The reported execution comparison is between the cardinality parser and the single-output parser. Entropy appears in the ambiguity-F1 comparison, but no unambiguous execution-accuracy value for entropy is given here.
And ‘matched’ means both sides of that execution comparison were at 91%, not merely close?

Yes. As reported, unambiguous execution accuracy matched the single-output parser at 91%: both figures in that comparison are 91%. The statement does not give finer-grained values beyond the reported percentage.
Can I say cardinality scored 0.87 on each of the five seeds?

No. The result is reported across five COGS-AMB seeds, but it does not list a score for each seed. Likewise, the 0.74 F1 and 91% accuracy should not be presented as separate per-seed values without that information.
Do we know whether the reported figures are means?

The statement does not specify an aggregation method. You can say the figures are reported across five seeds, but calling them means, medians, or values from a particular seed would add a detail not supplied here.
What can these numbers tell us about genuine ambiguity versus model uncertainty?

They show that, in the reported five-seed COGS-AMB comparison, cardinality-based detection had higher ambiguity F1 than entropy-based detection: 0.87 versus 0.74. That is consistent with a better measured distinction in this evaluation. The numbers alone do not identify which particular utterances each approach classified correctly or incorrectly.
So I shouldn’t claim every high-entropy error was handled correctly by cardinality?

Correct. An aggregate F1 score does not establish that every high-entropy error was handled correctly, or that every genuinely ambiguous utterance was recognized. It reports overall ambiguity-detection performance for the comparison given.
